checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: A hot on-sale opens. Two users click the same seat in the same millisecond.

options.label: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
options.verdict: Correct, and it is what most candidates reach for. The problem is duration: the lock is held while the user types their card details, so a row is pinned for minutes and the connection pool drains under a 10M-user spike.

options.label: Redis lock with TTL
options.sub: SET NX PX on seat id
options.verdict: The reservation becomes a short-lived key that expires on its own. A crashed service or an abandoned checkout releases the seat without a human, and Postgres only sees a write at confirmation.

defend.prompt: What does the TTL approach still owe you?

options.label: Postgres must still enforce uniqueness at confirm time
A slow user can lose the seat mid-checkout
Redis becomes a correctness dependency, not just a cache
It removes the need for a seat status column

defend.explain: Redis is the fast path, never the record. The final INSERT still has to be conditional, or a Redis failover hands the same seat to two people.

checkpoints.title: Capacity ladder

rungs.note: 100:1 means almost everything is reads — and reads are cacheable in a way bookings are not.
~500ms p95 for search; seat reservation is tighter at ~200ms.
Only the booking write. Everything else can be stale for seconds without anyone noticing.

checkpoints.explain: The 100:1 ratio is permission to cache aggressively everywhere except the one write that must never double-sell.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.prompt: Build the browse path so an on-sale surge never touches the booking database.
checkpoints.explain: Event pages and search are served from the CDN and Elasticsearch, so the millions of browsers never reach Postgres. Booking Service, Redis holds and Postgres are the write path — deliberately a separate, much narrower pipe.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: Seat maps are stale by minutes during an on-sale. Bookings are fine.
checkpoints.explain: The hit rate went up, which looks like a win and is actually the bug. Seat availability got cached with the same long TTL as static event metadata, so the CDN is now confidently serving sold seats. Availability needs a very short TTL or no caching at all; the event page around it can stay cached for hours.

wrong.Booking Service: Bookings are succeeding — the write path is healthy. The lie is on the read path.
wrong.Elasticsearch: Search is serving the documents it was given; nobody has told it seats changed.
wrong.Postgres primary: Postgres holds the truth. The question is who is not asking it.
